item.title: BCIC chairman warns of strict action against fertilizer irregularities
item.description:
Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation (BCIC) Chairman Md Babul Mia has warned of strict action against anyone involved in irregularities or corruption in fertilizer distribution and storage in the northern region.
He has also assured farmers that the country has adequate fertilizer stocks and there is no actual shortage.
Babul Mia made the remarks at a meeting of the monitoring committee on fertilizer transportation, storage and stock management at Rangpur Circuit House on November 13, said a press release.
The meeting, organised by the Rangpur district administration, was chaired by Rangpur Deputy Commissioner Israt Jahan. It focused on the progress of the project to construct 34 buffer warehouses and the current fertilizer stock, transportation and storage situation in the region.
Earlier, on November 12 and 13, the BCIC chairman visited under-construction buffer warehouses in Thakurgaon, Panchagarh, Lalmonirhat and Rangpur to assess the project's progress and the overall fertilizer supply situation.
During the visits, he inspected construction work and reviewed fertilizer transportation, storage and stock management at the sites.
He instructed the contractors and officials concerned to maintain construction quality and complete the work within the stipulated timeframe.
He also stressed the need to maintain adequate stocks in line with farmers' demand and ensure close monitoring of transportation and distribution to keep fertilizer supplies uninterrupted.
Addressing the meeting, Babul Mia said the government was taking all necessary measures to strengthen fertilizer supply and storage facilities in the northern region.
He warned that anyone involved in fertilizer-related irregularities or corruption would be brought to justice.
He said misleading claims about an artificial fertilizer shortage, spread by unscrupulous quarters, were creating confusion among farmers.
To prevent rumours and ensure transparency, he urged district administrations and officials concerned to regularly monitor fertilizer stocks and distribution.
He also advised farmers not to panic or stockpile more fertilizer than they need.

item.title: BADC project targets higher pulse, oilseed production
item.description:
The Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) is implementing a project to boost domestic production of pulses and oilseeds, reduce import dependence and strengthen the country's food and nutritional security.
According to a press release, the country's annual demand for pulses is 2.5 million tonnes, while domestic production stands at only 937,000 tonnes. Similarly, annual demand for edible oil is 2.482 million tonnes, against domestic production of 1.064 million tonnes, according to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE).
The shortfall forces Bangladesh to import substantial quantities of pulses and edible oil, putting pressure on foreign currency reserves.
Approved by the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (Ecnec) on December 8, 2024, the project, titled "Strengthening Sustainable Nutritional Security through the Production of Pulses and Oilseeds (Phase 2)," will run from July 2025 to June 2029.
The project aims to produce 18,000 tonnes of quality seeds and distribute them among farmers. Its activities cover 42 districts, two city corporations and 200 upazilas across eight divisions through three farms, three seed processing centres and 12 contract-farming zones.
Project estimates suggest that the targeted seed production will generate an additional 256,499 tonnes of agricultural produce worth Tk2,964 crore over the project's duration.
During the 2025-26 fiscal year, the project produced 3,723.112 tonnes of pulse and oilseed seeds through contract farming. These included lentil, mung bean, mustard, soybean, groundnut and sunflower seeds, which are being distributed for the 2026-27 cropping season.
Their use is expected to generate an additional 51,455 tonnes of crops worth Tk597.57 crore across approximately 606,360 acres.
The project, costing Tk265.78 crore, also includes training for 2,000 contract farmers in seed production, processing and storage.
Project Director Dr Md Shafiqul Islam is overseeing implementation, including field-level activities and seed production and distribution.
The initiative is expected to increase farmers' incomes, create rural employment and reduce the country's reliance on imported pulses and edible oil.

item.title: Satkhira municipality fails to ensure safe water for households
item.description:
Residents of Satkhira municipality have complained that the water supplied by the local authorities is often contaminated with dirt, foul-smelling substances, and even worms, making it unfit for drinking and household use.
Many families are consequently forced to spend Tk1,500-2,000 a month buying drinking water. Against this backdrop, civil society representatives have proposed eight recommendations to address the crisis, particularly in low-income communities.
The proposals include making water supply services affordable, promoting rooftop rainwater harvesting and household wells, developing rainwater reservoirs, and installing public water taps in slums and densely populated areas.
They also called for protecting ponds and other water bodies from encroachment, regularly testing municipal and jarred water for arsenic, iron, salinity and pH levels, and publishing the results online.
The recommendations were presented at a citizens' dialogue titled “Safe Drinking Water Crisis among Low-income Urban Communities and Ways Forward”, organised by research organisation Barcik at the Mangrove Conference Hall in Satkhira town yesterday.
Satkhira Green Coalition President Abu Affan Roj Babu chaired the event, while municipal Water Supply Engineer Nimai Chandra Pal attended as the chief guest.
At the dialogue, Baddipur Colony residents Jahanara Khatun and Mariam Khatun said their neighbourhood remains waterlogged for nearly six months during the rainy season, causing an acute shortage of drinking water. Many households have yet to receive municipal water connections despite living within the city.
Professor Pabitra Mohan Das said he spends Tk1,600-1,700 a month buying jarred water for drinking and cooking. With an adequate municipal supply, the same needs could be met for around Tk200, he added.

item.title: 40 factories shut in Savar-Ashulia industrial belt amid labour unrest
item.description:
A group of workers gathered at Padmar Mor in Savar’s Hemayetpur around 3pm on Monday, briefly drawing attention to the area. Police later asked them to disperse peacefully, and they left the road shortly afterwards without further incident.
Meanwhile, around 40 factories remained closed in the Savar and Ashulia industrial areas on Monday, according to industrial police.
Of the closed factories, 27 were shut under Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, while nine were declared closed indefinitely. The remaining factories were observing general holidays.
Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of police (SP) of Ashulia Industrial Police-1, said workers at one factory refused to resume work after the lunch break and remained seated inside the premises. The factory authorities subsequently declared a holiday, he added.
Workers at two other factories also stopped working and remained seated, the SP said.
However, workers at other factories across the industrial areas continued their work peacefully, he added.

item.title: Icon Ronaldinho makes winning return to pro football in Italy's third division
item.description:
Greying and rounder in the face than during his prime, Ronaldinho made a winning return to professional football on Sunday for Ravenna, an ambitious club in Italy's third tier aiming to reach Serie A.
Under the watchful eye of Ignazio Cipriani, the Italian-American businessman who has owned the club since 2024, Ronaldinho perfectly played his role as the centrepiece of a clever PR stunt.
The 46-year-old Brazilian great put in a low-key performance in his first competitive match since playing for Fluminense in 2015, as Ravenna, bidding for promotion to Serie B, beat local rivals Forli 2-0 in front of a packed Stadio Bruno Benelli on Italy's Adriatic coast.
Known for his dynamic dribbling and often outrageous ball control in his heyday, Ronaldinho largely strolled around the pitch and laid off simple passes to his teammates, who would once upon a time not have been anywhere near his level as players.
Ronaldinho's arrival has given Ravenna a previously unimaginable profile, and Cipriani would no doubt have been delighted to see the pack of reporters and photographers that descended on the Benelli.
The 2005 Ballon d'Or winner only played in the first half but was involved in the move which ended with Giulio Donati smashing hosts Ravenna ahead in the 36th minute.
Ronaldinho entered the field to great fanfare, with the 5,000-capacity Benelli having a temporary stand with 1,800 places -- dubbed "R10" -- added for the occasion.
Flares and smoke bombs were let off in the stands while Andrea Bocelli's "Con Te Partiro" blasting out of the stadium's speakers.
And he left after the first half, but not before plenty of handshakes with his teammates and match officials.
Only he knows whether he will play for Ravenna again, although he had only taken part in a single training session with his teammates before this one-off appearance.
He only arrived in Italy a few days before Sunday's match, suggesting that he hasn't committed himself for the long haul.
Ravenna, who have not even played in Serie B since 2008, are second in their regional group in Serie C and came into the weekend's fixtures six points behind leaders Spezia.
One team for each of the three groups will be directly promoted to Serie B, with the final spot in the second tier decided.

item.title: Kroupi on target as France clinch Nations League quarters spot
item.description:
Eli Junior Kroupi scored his first France goal as Les Bleus beat Turkey 2-1 on Sunday to secure a spot in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Nations League.
France needed a draw in their last Group A1 outing to make sure of their progress to the quarter-finals next March, and they went ahead just after half-time in Bordeaux via an Emirhan Topcu own goal.
Bournemouth forward Kroupi, 20, replaced Bradley Barcola just past the hour and made it 2-0 from a Rayan Cherki assist, before Abdulkerim Bardakci pulled one back for Turkey at the death.
"At first I thought I was offside, but when I saw the goal had been given it was an incredible feeling," Kroupi, who has only just returned after missing the first two months of the season due to injury, told broadcaster TF1.
"Of course I was thinking about my injury. I hope I have left all that behind me and I can look forward now."
The result allowed Zinedine Zidane's French side to bounce back from a 3-1 loss away to Italy on Thursday as they finish on top of their group with 13 points, one point ahead of Belgium.
The Belgians also progress into the quarter-finals after coming from behind to thrash Italy 4-1 in Brussels.
France, who won the Nations League in 2021, are therefore guaranteed to play a runner-up from one of the other groups in League A in the quarters, the draw for which will take place this coming Friday.
World Cup winners Spain are among their potential opponents in the last eight.
"Our objective was to qualify, ideally in first place, so we have achieved our goal, but I was a bit perplexed with our performance," admitted Zidane.
"We rectified certain things at half-time, got our foot on the ball and were better in the second half, but there are things we still need to improve."
France have been hit by a host of injury issues, with last year's Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembele among the many players missing for Zidane just now.
Captain Kylian Mbappe did return, however, after missing France's last four matches since scoring the winner in Turkey on Zidane's debut in September.
"I think he deserved to score a hat-trick today given the number of chances he had. I also liked the way he played without the ball. He played the role of captain marvellously," Zidane said of the Real Madrid superstar.
This game carried special significance for Zidane, who made his name as a player at Bordeaux in the 1990s before moving to Juventus and inspiring France to World Cup glory in 1998.
His return to the south-western city risked being spoiled by the performance of Turkey goalkeeper Berke Ozer, who frustrated France with a host of saves.
However, the home side went ahead in the 49th minute when Adrien Rabiot helped on a corner and Besiktas defender Topcu only succeeded in putting the ball over the line.
Kroupi, who scored 13 goals in the Premier League last season for Bournemouth, was handed a late call-up by Zidane after Marcus Thuram pulled out injured at the start of last week.
He won his first cap off the bench against Italy and notched his first France goal in the 80th minute here after combining superbly with Cherki.
That goal proved to be decisive as Bardakci replied in the 90th minute for Turkey, who finish with six defeats from six games.

item.title: Zverev too strong for debutant Jodar in ATP Finals
item.description:
World number one Alexander Zverev cruised through his opening match at the season-ending ATP Finals on Sunday, beating Spanish debutant Rafael Jodar 6–4, 6–4.
In the evening, American third seed Ben Shelton beat Frenchman Arthur Fils, seeded seventh, 6-2, 3-6, 6-3.
Zverev, who won the tournament in 2018 and 2021, needed just one hour and 27 minutes to overcome the season's breakout star.
Ranked 11th in the world, the 20-year-old Jodar is making his debut at the elite eight-player tournament.
Zverev had been eliminated in his opening match at the Paris Masters -- the final Masters 1000 event of the year -- and endured a lacklustre autumn as he blamed mental and physical exhaustion.
However, with 10 aces and a strong return of serve he stifled Jodar, who dropped his serve in the seventh game of the first set and again in the third game of the second.
"It wasn't the perfect match, but I'm happy; it's a great start to the tournament for me," Zverev said.
"With a 6-4, 6-4 win...against a Top 8 player in the world. You take that, for sure. I'm happy with the start, but I know I have to improve still."
In the other match in the John McEnroe group, Shelton secured his first-ever victory at the tournament. His debut appearance in 2025 ended with three defeats.
"It means a lot," Shelton said. "Especially doing it in the first match of the round robin, giving myself a little bit of momentum."
In the first set, Shelton overpowered Fils, the first Frenchman to qualify for the ATP Finals in 10 years.
The 22-year-old Fils then began to extend rallies. He forced his first break point of the match in eighth game and took it. He then saved two break points in the next game to tie the match.
Serving for the match in the final set, Shelton faced two break points but saved them with ferocious aces before pounding his way to the win with booming forehands.
"That was really intense, especially in the first set," Shelton said. "I don't know that I've played that many rallies out there on tour on a court this fast. So it was physical, really physical. A tough contest."
"I was breathing hard after pretty much every point, and I'm excited to get started in a match like that. Everything wasn't perfect, but my overall level was good and I thought it was a great match I will be able to build on this week."
He will face Zverev on Tuesday.
Zverev secured the world number one ranking in early November after winning his first two Grand Slam titles in 2026, but the 29-year-old is not necessarily the favourite in Turin.
Spaniard Carlos Alcaraz, ranked third in the world, who plays American Frances Tiafoe on Monday, is considered the favourite following his comeback from a wrist injury with three wins in five tournaments -- Tokyo, Vienna and the Paris Masters.
Italy's Jannik Sinner won the last two editions of the Finals but he has not played since winning Wimbledon in July due to a knee injury.

item.title: Andreeva defeats Svitolina to win WTA Finals
item.description:
Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva battled past Elina Svitolina in straight sets to win the season-ending WTA Finals crown on Sunday.
Andreeva powered to a 7-5, 6-3 victory in a hard-fought duel in Indian Wells to complete a superb week in California.
Reigning French Open champion Andreeva, 19, clinched the title without dropping a set in the tournament.
She is only the third teenager after Chris Evert and Maria Sharapova to win the WTA Finals on their debut.
"It feels amazing, of course I'm super-privileged to put my name in that group," said Andreeva.
The teenager thanked friends, family and support staff in a victory speech, before light-heartedly thanking herself for her success.
"I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work, for never quitting, for always believing in myself, for not taking the days off, for working every day, and for committing to what I have to do," said Andreeva, wearing a track-suit top with the slogan "I want to thank myself."
A grueling 1hr 48min duel saw Andreeva secure a break in the opening game of the first set before holding for a 2-0 lead.
Ukrainian veteran Svitolina broke back in the fourth game, conjuring a sublime angled volley to level at 2-2.
Svitolina was soon back under pressure though, conceding another break to go 4-3 down before Andreeva held for a 5-3 lead.
There was more drama to follow when Andreeva served for the first set at 5-4 up.
She opened with back-to-back double faults to go 0-30 down, and then yanked a wild forehand wide to give Svitolina two break points at 15-40.
A long forehand gave Svitolina the break to knot it at 5-5 but Andreeva hit back immediately with her third break of serve to regain the advantage at 6-5.
The Russian made no mistake when serving for the set for a second time, holding comfortably to go 1-0 up.
The second set followed a familiar pattern, with both players trading some brutal groundstrokes in a series of long rallies.
Andreeva broke to take the lead at 1-0 but Svitolina responded in a marathon second game, breaking back after converting her seventh break point to level at 1-1.
Andreeva edged back in front with a break to go 3-2 up and then held for a 4-2 lead.
The next two games went with serve to leave Svitolina serving to stay in the match at 5-3 down.
A fortunate net cord left Andreeva with three match points at 0-40.
Svitolina saved the first and looked poised to save another, only to hit a wide open overhead smash into the net to give Andreeva the win.
Svitolina, who had been thumped 6-4, 6-0 by Andreeva in the opening round-robin game of the tournament, took positives from her performance.
"After the first match I was not expecting to play in the final," Svitolina said. "Unfortunately it didn't go my way but I gave it my all."

item.title: Belgium smash Italy to reach Nations League quarters
item.description:
Belgium thumped Italy 4-1 to join France in the Nations League quarter-finals.
Sitting third in Group A1 ahead of kick-off and needing a win to qualify for the last eight, Belgium had their backs up against the wall when Francesco Pio Esposito volleyed Italy ahead in the 11th minute.
But Belgium blew Italy away in the following quarter of an hour, with Maxim De Cuyper and Nathan Ngoy bundling the hosts ahead before Jeremy Doku slalomed through the Azzurri defence and confidently shot home.
Mark van Bommel's team deservedly claimed a spot in the quarters and made sure the scoreline reflected the balance of play when one of many attacks against an open Italy defence ended with Diego Moreira slotting home with 10 minutes remaining.
A dismal night for Italy, who were top of the group after beating France last time out and just needed a draw to go through, was made even worse when Senne Lammens saved Esposito's weak late penalty.
"Nights like this can happen, unfortunately. These things can happen during a rebuilding process," said Italy boss Roberto Mancini.
"We're disappointed, but this is the kind of night that will ultimately prove useful to us."
France top the group after bouncing back from defeat to Italy with a 2-1 win over rock-bottom Turkey in Bordeaux.
Les Bleus will head into the draw for the last eight, scheduled for Friday in Nyon, Switzerland, as a seeded team, a position that ensures they will host the return leg in March 2027 but could mean they face Spain.
An Emirhan Topcu own goal just after half-time and Eli Junior Kroupi's first goal for France were enough for Zinedine Zidane's team to prevail and take top spot in the final round of of matches.

item.title: England beat Spain to end record unbeaten streak
item.description:
England snapped world champions Spain's record unbeaten run with a 3-2 victory in Madrid on Sunday to clinch the top spot in Nations League group A3.
Goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White inflicted La Roja's first loss in a competitive game since March 2023, after 44 without defeat.
England's Elliot Anderson was sent off in the second half as Spain fought back from three goals down with strikes from Mikel Oyarzabal and Nico Williams, but Luis de la Fuente's World Cup winners could not find the equaliser.
Both sides were already sure to progress, but as group winners England will be seeded for the quarter-finals in March.
Spain had beaten England in the Euro 2024 final before adding a second world crown this summer, while the Three Lions finished third.
"We knew we were going to beat them tonight, the message from the manager after the Croatia game (on Thursday) has been so positive," England midfielder Declan Rice told ITV.
"The first 10 minutes was the best we've played."
England coach Thomas Tuchel hailed his team on their superb performance in the Spanish capital.
"We brought everything to the table," Tuchel told ITV.
"We were brave. Spirit wise, energy wise and also football quality was (all at the) highest level."
Tuchel selected James Trafford in goal over Jordan Pickford and also brought White and Konsa into the side.
Teenage star Lamine Yamal was fit to start for Spain at Atletico Madrid's Metropolitano stadium after missing their midweek win over the Czech Republic.
However the youngster did not see much of the ball in the first half as England came out strongly.
Spain goalkeeper Unai Simon produced a strong reaction save to deny Jude Bellingham, while Anthony Gordon had a dangerous shot blocked.
Ballon d'Or winner Kane, who beat Yamal to the award, sent an effort narrowly wide.
Barcelona defender Pau Cubarsi handed England the advantage when he clumsily felled Kane in the area on the stroke of half time.
The Bayern Munich hitman powered a perfect penalty past Simon, who dived the right way but to no avail.
De la Fuente tried to react at half-time with a triple change, including throwing on Barcelona duo Fermin Lopez and Pedri, but England quickly found more joy.
Konsa headed home the second from Declan Rice's corner in the 53rd minute after the Arsenal defender was left unmarked by Spain's defence.
Four minutes later England sliced open Spain's defence with Kane and Bellingham combining to set up White for the third.
La Roja clawed their way back into the game when Anderson fouled Yamal in the area as the Spain striker ran in on goal.
The Manchester City midfielder was dismissed and Oyarzabal slotted home the penalty.
Spain found a second when Gordon gave the ball away and Yamal fed Williams, whose shot hit the post and bounced in.
Williams curled over and Trafford superbly denied Yamal and Marc Cucurella as Spain looked fruitlessly for the goal they needed to preserve their unbeaten record.
Including friendlies, Spain had gone 43 straight matches without defeat.
"On the pitch everything happens very fast, it's a pity," Oyarzabal told TVE about England's two goals early in the second half.
"You have to focus on what came after, the reaction -- the team never stopped pushing, never stopped trying... their goalkeeper also deserves credit for us not having equalised."

item.title: Zero tolerance for emboldened criminals
item.description:
The 30-minute rampage inside Durbin Bangla restaurant in Mohakhali, simply because an individual was asked to wait for a table, is simply unacceptable. That this escalated to assault of the staff, looting cash, ripping out CCTV hard drives, and inflicting up to Tk30 lakh in damages is infuriating.
That very same night, helmeted gunmen opened fire on Anurag Pharmacy on Mohammadpur's Babar Road -- barely 500 metres from a deputy police commissioner's office -- narrowly missing a sales employee’s head following repeated crude bomb blasts and an extortion demand.
Such incidents cannot be taken as isolated aberrations but rather must be seen as symptoms of a growing culture of impunity tightening and of criminals who have been emboldened due to a lack of consequences for their actions.
When armed extortionists can casually shoot up a busy storefront, and entitled thugs can systematically destroy a thriving restaurant in broad daylight without immediate consequences, the message sent to citizens and business owners is chilling: No one is safe, and criminals no longer fear the state.
What is most troubling is the sluggish, reactive posture of law enforcement. Routine assurances that "investigations are underway" are cold comfort to terrorized workers and entrepreneurs watching their livelihoods shattered.
The state cannot afford to turn a blind eye to escalating urban insecurity or treat violent extortion and mob vandalism as routine policing matters. Protecting life, property, and commercial activity is the most basic obligation of the state.
It’s time to enforce an uncompromising, zero-tolerance policy against street thuggery, political muscle-flexing, and armed extortion. Law enforcement too must hold negligent officers accountable for delayed interventions.
Our capital’s residents and businesses deserve a capital governed by the rule of law and not surrendered to the whims of vandals and gunmen.

item.title: Stop making citizens pay
item.description:
To say that Bangladesh’s banking sector is being drowned by non-performing loans (NPLs) would be a laughable understatement at this point.
With the default loan rate hitting a staggering 32.78%, nearly one out of every three taka disbursed across the country's financial system is now non-performing.
Worse still, many analysts are saying what many have long feared: There is virtually zero chance of recovering 80-90% of these toxic assets.
That the overwhelming majority of this crisis is the direct result of operational failures, procedural sabotage, and outright financial crimes should leave every person in this country fuming.
While full-fledged Islamic banks stagger under a 58.9% default rate and state-owned lenders bleed at 43.2%, willful defaulters continue to exploit court injunctions, currently blocking the recovery of Tk 182,419 crore across 845 pending lawsuits to shield stolen public wealth.
It is entirely unacceptable that ordinary depositors, honest entrepreneurs, and taxpayers are continuously forced to absorb the consequences of such gross impunity.
When banks are starved of liquidity by corporate looters, legitimate businesses face suffocating borrowing costs. In addition, our private sector credit growth has collapsed to dismal lows, and savers continue to watch their hard-earned deposits trapped in dysfunctional institutions.
Tackling such a predicament has long been beyond the capacity of banks alone and the government and the central bank must do better. We must end this cycle of opaque half-measures and taxpayer-funded bailouts.
This starts with regular public disclosures on cash recoveries, capital adequacy, and above all, revealing the identities of top willful defaulters. In addition, independent audits and bank-specific resolution frameworks must be enforced without political interference.
Fixing the banking sector cannot mean endlessly penalizing the general public. The state must hold the ones who broke our banks accountable.

item.title: Global climate justice movement calls for accountability, democracy beyond COP31
item.description:
A global coalition of climate activists, civil society organizations and social movements has called for stronger climate accountability, democratic participation and a just transition away from fossil fuel-dependent economies at the Peoples' Climate Summit Beyond COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.
The summit, being held from November 14 to 18 at the Mimar Sinan Congress Center, has brought together representatives of social movements, Indigenous peoples, workers, farmers, fisherfolk, youth and environmental justice organizations from around the world to demand urgent action on the climate crisis.
At the opening session on November 15, speakers highlighted the growing gap between developed countries' financial and climate commitments and the mounting impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.
Among those addressing the session were Sharif Jamil, global board member of Waterkeeper Alliance; Tasneem Essop, president of Climate Action Network (CAN) International; Tomo Iwabuchi, a member of the Japanese Communist Party; social scientist Markus Wissen; and Ecehan Balta of the Peoples' Climate Summit.
The speakers stressed that tackling climate change requires more than government pledges, calling for global solidarity, people's participation and a fundamental transformation of the economic systems driving environmental destruction.
Sharif Jamil called for adequate climate finance, including loss and damage funding in the form of reparations, arguing that countries and communities suffering the consequences of climate change should not be left to bear the costs of a crisis they did little to create.
Referring to the devastating 2024 floods in Feni, Bangladesh, recent heavy rainfall in Istanbul and Bangkok, and extreme heat that disrupted people's lives during London Climate Week, he questioned who should be held responsible for the growing climate-related disasters.
He also asked how affected communities would be compensated for their losses and demanded effective mechanisms to ensure accountability, particularly from countries in the Global North.
His remarks underscored the longstanding demand of climate-vulnerable countries for developed nations to fulfil their historical responsibilities through predictable, adequate and accessible climate finance.
Tasneem Essop criticized the growing militarization and conflicts across the world, arguing that governments capable of mobilizing enormous resources for warfare have repeatedly failed to fulfil their climate commitments and responsibilities.
She questioned the contradiction between the international community's ability to mobilize resources for military operations and its failure to provide adequate support to communities facing climate disasters.
Essop called for stronger people's movements across the world to pressure governments to take meaningful action in international climate negotiations, including at COP31.
She emphasized that civil society and grassroots movements must remain active in demanding accountability from governments and ensuring that climate negotiations respond to people's needs.
The summit seeks to strengthen international cooperation among grassroots movements opposing fossil fuel expansion, wars and militarization, corporate-controlled food systems and the destruction of ecosystems.
Participants are also demanding climate justice, accountability for historical emissions, repayment of climate debt and a transition towards economic systems that priorities human rights, environmental protection and social equality.
The gathering began on November 14 with a march through Antalya as part of the Global Day of Action. Discussions, solidarity-building activities and collective actions are scheduled to continue until November 18.
The summit is taking place alongside the COP31 climate conference, providing a platform for communities and movements to advance demands that they say remain inadequately addressed in formal international climate negotiations.
Organizers and participants are seeking to ensure that the voices of communities most affected by climate change are central to decisions on climate finance, energy transition, environmental protection and global climate governance.

item.title: Can a ‘coalition of the willing’ speed up a fossil fuel phaseout?
item.description:
This time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal. More than 80 countries backed the idea.
But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a “voluntary” roadmap. At the same time, a group of 57 countries frustrated with the deadlock at the consensus-based UN talks decided to form a “coalition of the willing” to accelerate the fossil fuel exit outside the COP framework.
They held their own summit in April in Santa Marta, Colombia — the first such conference to specifically focus on implementing the transition away from fossil fuels (referred to as TAFF).
Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, the Santa Marta conference brought together countries including Canada, Norway, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico, Australia and Germany, as well as highly climate-vulnerable states such as Vanuatu.
The idea was for governments to start developing national roadmaps and working out how to restructure their financial and trade systems to wean themselves off polluting energy sources — an incredibly complicated undertaking, particularly for developing countries dependent on revenue from fossil fuel exports.
Part of their discussions focused on cutting subsidies for oil, coal and gas, as well as supporting people whose livelihoods rely on the fossil fuel industry to find new forms of income.
A little over six months on from the Santa Marta meeting, representatives from almost 200 countries are holding talks in Antalya, Turkiye, as part of the latest UN climate conference.
Countries agreed for the first time in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver behind rising global temperatures. But summits since then have failed to pin down how to implement that pledge.
It’s not yet clear whether the Santa Marta coalition will influence ambition at this year’s COP.
“I think it’s more of a long-term game,” said Chetna Hareesh Kumar, a climate policy analyst at the Berlin-based research organization NewClimate Institute.
She says it’s too soon to expect the coalition to have an influence on the negotiations but adds that that could change at future COPs. The grouping could bring more nations on board if, for example, it shows it can be truly inclusive, address the needs of different types of countries and show that a transition is feasible.
One role the group is playing, according to Alexandra Scott, a senior climate diplomacy adviser at Italian climate change think tank Eccp, is “keeping up the political momentum,” and showing “that there is this huge group of countries who really want to accelerate this transition away from fossil fuels.”
She says it’s also building an invaluable “cadre of knowledge” on how to develop national Taff plans and deal with barriers individual countries face — like how to secure funding for the infrastructure investments needed for the energy transition.
The Santa Marta group is “really answering a lot of the questions that countries have always had on how on earth do we even start to transition our whole economy off fossil fuels?” Scott said.
This expertise being shared and tested in practice can show what such a transformation could look like and the knowledge brought into COP, added Scott.
Since the Santa Marta conference, Germany, France and the Netherlands have released national plans to phase out fossil fuels. While the plans contain no new commitments, experts see them as a positive first step.
Kumar says more countries could announce similar plans just ahead of the second Taff summit in Tuvalu next year. Finland presented its Taff roadmap in the first week of COP, but analysts do not expect many more countries to follow suit soon.
Another potential boost that could get momentum going is Brazil’s recently published global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, promised at last year’s COP.
The nearly 200-page document seeks to serve as a toolkit for countries shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. It envisages countries making a phased transition between 2028 and 2033.
The aim, Ana Toni, CEO of last year’s COP, told AP, is to break down the transition into “smaller actionable solutions” and help countries make practical progress.
The roadmap suggests measures tailored to each country’s circumstances, including dependence on fossil fuel and financial capacities. “Levers” it proposes include reducing fossil fuel subsidies, expanding renewable energy and cutting methane emissions.
Kumar called it a “customizable” approach that allows every country to take action, regardless of its situation. “The question really is now what countries do with it and how much momentum they can generate,” she added.
This year’s climate change summit in Turkiye — taking place after a series of deadly heat waves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people — isn’t expected to result in any big announcements about fossil fuels.
Global renewable energy capacity has surged in recent years, making up a third of the world’s power generation for the first time in 2025. But many countries still rely on coal, oil and gas.
A database compiled by the German environmental organization Urgewald shows that most oil and gas companies worldwide, among them QatarEnergy, Saudi Aramco and Russia’s Gazprom, are exploring or developing new reserves.
Meanwhile, subsidies for fossil fuels amount to around $920 billion per year, according to data from the Oecd, but that number is falling.
One issue Turkiye is pushing at the COP conference is electrification. It’s calling on countries to endorse the goal of 35% of final energy consumption coming from electricity by 2035 — up from around 20% today.
The pledge has drawn criticism from some circles, though, for leaving open whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources.
Ideally, Kumar said, electrification would be powered by renewables and tied to a goal of phasing out polluting fossil fuels.
“If something like that could make it to the final text, that would be a really good sign for momentum.”

item.title: 17 killed in two mass shootings in South Africa
item.description:
Seventeen people have been killed in two separate shootings in South Africa, police said on Monday, as the crime-weary country battles persistently high murder rates.
Roughly 60 people are killed in the country on average a day, according to police statistics, with motives ranging from the drugs trade and illegal mining to competition over minibus taxi routes.
In one incident, nine bodies were found early Monday in an informal settlement outside the capital Pretoria, police said.
“All nine were found in a shack with gunshot wounds this morning,” a spokeswoman said.
The dead were six men and three women.
The second killing occurred in a semi-rural area outside the eastern city of Pietermaritzburg where police found a bullet-riddled vehicle after responding to reports of a shooting late Sunday.
“Inside the vehicle police found eight men who had multiple gunshot wounds and were certified dead at the scene,” a police statement said.
The men had not yet been identified and it was too early to speculate on a motive, KwaZulu-Natal province police spokesman Colonel Robert Netshiunda told the Newzroom Afrika broadcaster.
“We have seen these kinds of shootings before and there have been different motives from stock theft-related, to drugs-related to taxi violence,” he said.

item.title: Kremlin slams Zelensky for divulging US land-for-Nato offer
item.description:
Russia on Monday criticized Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky for revealing Washington had proposed that Kyiv cede land for Nato membership as part of a possible peace deal with Moscow.
The Kremlin did not confirm the proposal had been made or comment on it. But Moscow has long opposed Ukraine joining the US-led military alliance.
“We continue to maintain our position that it is inadvisable to disclose details of the discussions taking place between us and the Americans in the interests of the peace process,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters, including AFP.
Zelensky had told journalists on Friday that the offer had been made by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who last week held talks in Abu Dhabi with both sides, before separate meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky.
“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelensky said.
Kyiv has long pushed for Nato membership hoping its mutual defense clauses will be a guarantee against a future Russian attack.
But Moscow has for years railed against new countries joining Nato -- believing it was promised by the United States that that alliance would not move closer to its borders.
Since it launched its full-scale offensive on Ukraine in 2022, both Sweden and Finland - which has a 1,300-kilometre (800-mile) border with Russia -- have joined Nato.

item.title: Dhaka Board extends HSC supplementary exam form deadline by 3 days
item.description:
The Dhaka Education Board has extended the deadline for filling out examination forms for the 2026 Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) supplementary examination by three days.
Under the revised schedule, students can fill out their forms until November 18, while the deadline for paying examination fees has been extended to November 19.
Dhaka Education Board Controller of Examinations Professor Jesmin Taslima Banu announced the extension in a notice on Sunday.
According to the notice, students can complete the form-filling process between November 16 and 18, while examination fees must be paid through Sonali Bank by November 19.

item.title: White sofas and tables getting dirty too quickly? Here's what to do
item.description:
Dust, fingerprints, food stains, and moisture can quickly make white furniture look dull and dirty, particularly in humid weather. However, keeping white furniture in good condition requires more than regular cleaning. Experts say maintenance methods should vary depending on the material used.
Momin Hossain, an interior designer at interior design firm Double Zero Space, says regular dusting with a dry cloth is one of the most important steps in maintaining white furniture.
"Keeping white furniture clean every day with a dry cloth is particularly important. With proper care according to the material, white furniture can retain its appearance for years," he says.
Duco paint is applied to wooden surfaces using a spray technique, giving furniture a smooth and glossy finish. Although white is a popular choice for creating a fresh and soothing interior, Duco paint is available in a wide range of colors.
For Duco-painted furniture, begin by removing dust with a soft, dry cotton cloth. Regular dusting prevents dirt from accumulating on the surface.
A deeper clean can be carried out once a month. Mix a small amount of soap with room-temperature water, dampen a soft cloth with the solution, and gently wipe the furniture. Immediately afterwards, use a dry cloth to remove any remaining moisture, ensuring no water is left on the surface.
Duco-painted furniture should be kept away from direct sunlight, excessive heat, and rain. Prolonged exposure to sunlight or water can affect the paint's shine and finish.
For example, if a dining table has a Duco finish, always use a heat-resistant mat or trivet underneath hot dishes instead of placing them directly on the surface. Following these precautions can help preserve the appearance of white Duco-painted furniture.
White furniture made from medium-density fibreboard (MDF) or other engineered wood also requires careful maintenance.
Start by removing dust with a dry cloth. For general cleaning, however, it is important to follow the manufacturer's recommendations, as excessive moisture can damage engineered wood.
For stubborn stains, use a soft cloth lightly dampened with water. Wring it out thoroughly before wiping the affected area, making sure water does not seep into the edges or joints of the board.
Once the stain has been removed, immediately wipe the surface with a dry cloth. Allowing moisture to accumulate can cause the edges of engineered wood furniture to swell.
White melamine-finished furniture is particularly common in modern households and is relatively easy to maintain. Regular dusting is generally sufficient to preserve its appearance.
For a deeper clean, avoid using abrasive or metal scrubbers. These can scratch the glossy finish, leaving visible marks and affecting the furniture's overall appearance.
White faux leather sofas and chairs require extra care, as their surfaces can be particularly vulnerable to stains and damage.
Begin by removing dust with a soft cloth or the soft-brush attachment of a vacuum cleaner. It is safest to use cleaning products specifically recommended by the manufacturer.
Avoid using strong alkaline cleaners or harsh chemicals without checking the product instructions, as they may damage the surface.
If tea, coffee, or another liquid spills onto the furniture, immediately blot it with a clean, dry cloth instead of rubbing the area. Rubbing can spread the stain and potentially damage the material.
Faux leather furniture should also be kept away from direct sunlight and excessive heat, which can affect its appearance over time.
White furniture tends to show dust and stains more visibly than darker pieces, making regular maintenance essential. Accumulated dirt can gradually take away its brightness and make even well-maintained interiors look dull.
However, choosing the right cleaning method for each material can help preserve the furniture's appearance and extend its lifespan.
If the surface becomes heavily stained or the finish deteriorates significantly, repainting or refinishing may be necessary. With proper care and timely maintenance, white furniture can retain its fresh appearance for years.

item.title: Can a tiny sticker really make an angry pimple disappear overnight?
item.description:
An important event is coming up, or perhaps a long-awaited meeting with someone special. But just the night before, an angry, painful pimple comes out on the face. In such situations, many people instinctively squeeze the spot to get rid of the pus. However, doing so can worsen redness and swelling, damage the skin, and leave behind stubborn scars.
To avoid such last-minute skin troubles, pimple patches have become increasingly popular, particularly among younger consumers.
A growing number of pimple patches from international brands are now available on the market. These small, transparent stickers come in different shapes and are designed to be placed directly over pimples. But do they actually help treat acne, or are they simply a temporary skincare solution?
According to beauty experts, pimple patches are not a permanent treatment for acne but can offer an effective short-term solution. They work by creating a protective barrier over the affected area, preventing further irritation and contact with external contaminants.
Most pimples contain fluid and pus that develop as a result of inflammation and infection. Pimple patches adhere to the skin and absorb excess fluid from the affected area.
One of their biggest advantages is that they cover the pimple, discouraging people from touching, picking, or squeezing it. This helps prevent the transfer of bacteria from the fingers, reducing the risk of further irritation and inflammation.
Many patches are also transparent, making them less noticeable when worn outside the home.
Kochi said pimple patches are not equally effective against all types of acne. They are primarily suitable for mild, active breakouts that appear on the surface of the skin.
However, they offer little benefit for deeper forms of acne, such as cystic acne, or persistent breakouts associated with hormonal imbalances. Such conditions generally require long-term treatment under the guidance of a dermatologist.
Pimple patches are available with different active ingredients, making it important to choose one that suits your skin type and specific concerns.
Oily skin: People with excessively oily, acne-prone skin may consider patches containing salicylic acid. The ingredient helps control excess sebum and clear clogged pores.
Sensitive and dry skin: Hydrocolloid patches are generally a suitable option for sensitive or dry skin. They help maintain a moist environment around the affected area, supporting the skin's natural healing process without causing unnecessary irritation.
Normal skin: For occasional breakouts on otherwise normal skin, patches containing tea tree oil may be an option. Tea tree oil is known for its antimicrobial properties and is commonly used in products designed for acne-prone skin.
The effectiveness of a pimple patch largely depends on how it is applied.
Before using one, the face should be thoroughly cleansed and dried. Applying a patch over skin covered with oil, moisturizer, or lotion can prevent it from adhering properly and reduce its effectiveness.
Once the skin is completely dry, place the patch directly over the affected spot. The rest of the skincare routine can then be continued as usual, avoiding the area covered by the patch.
The recommended duration of use is generally mentioned on the packaging and varies by brand. Depending on the product, patches may be worn for four, six, or 12 hours, or overnight.
Once the recommended time has passed, gently peel off the patch. Any fluid absorbed by the hydrocolloid material will be visible on its surface.
Pimple patches should never be applied to an unclean face or over makeup. Doing so can trap dirt and impurities against the skin and potentially aggravate irritation.
It is also important to remember that pimple patches are not a miracle cure for acne. While they can help protect individual breakouts and reduce the urge to pick at them, they cannot address the underlying causes of persistent acne.
For occasional breakouts, they can be a convenient way to protect the affected area and manage excess fluid. However, maintaining healthy skin requires a consistent skincare routine, a balanced diet, and healthy lifestyle habits. For recurring or severe acne, consulting a dermatologist remains the most effective approach to long-term treatment.

Is the govt hearing warning bells of a political catastrophe?
item.description:
The announcement that “Sheikh Hasina will return to the country in December” can no longer be dismissed as mere emotional wishful thinking. It is a clear text—and its subtext is now firmly established. Since the first week of November, crude bomb explosions, arson attacks on parked buses, road blockades at dawn, and flash processions by the banned organisation have become daily occurrences.

In Faridpur, bus driver Kalachand Sheikh burned to death in his sleep. In Netrokona, a train carriage was set ablaze. Crude bombs exploded on the Dhaka University campus. Grenade-like objects were recovered outside Rajshahi Airport. In Gopalganj, a police vehicle was overturned and torched. All of these are the subtext to the primary text. Deciphered, the core message is clear: a political catastrophe is knocking at the door. At this juncture, seeking answers to several critical questions is imperative.

Is a third party testing capabilities of intelligence agencies?

The concept of a “test case” must be kept in mind. In political sociology, concepts such as “probing” and “reconnaissance by fire” exist within discourses on military rule and insurgency. These signify measuring an adversary’s response through minor strikes before a major blow, low expenditure before heavy spending, and small investments before committing large-scale resources—much like tasting a curry for salt or pressing a grain of rice to check if it is cooked.

The objective of reconnaissance is not destruction, but intelligence gathering: How many minutes did it take the police to arrive? In which districts are law enforcement forces weak? Do intelligence agencies receive advance warnings? Who gets arrested—the masterminds or hired hands? Does the government overreact or remain indifferent? How effectively can the administration contain the fallout? How vocal are talk shows on the matter? How much traction do these incidents gain in newspapers? How terrified or apathetic is the public?

Suppose a domestic or international actor is actively seeking to ignite a civil war in a particular country. First, they will assess the viability. They will pay no heed to public resentment against the operatives they use to initiate the disruption; their sole objective is to gauge state capacity—observing how swiftly and accurately the state detects and suppresses violence. This insight is not mine, but that of political scientists James Fearon and David Laitin, who argue that testing an opponent’s capacity is a logical step in any organised violent enterprise.

The April 1975 bus attack in Ain el-Rammaneh is widely regarded as the spark that ignited the Lebanese Civil War. However, in the preceding months, various factions had tested the inaction and internal divisions of state forces through isolated skirmishes. Similarly, in Rwanda, three months prior to the genocide, reactions were measured through minor acts of violence and radio propaganda. In January 1994, UN peacekeeping force commander Roméo Dallaire sent a warning cable to New York reporting that lists of Tutsis were being compiled, weapons stockpiled, and militias trained. Ignoring that warning led to catastrophic consequences.

In Kenya, post-election violence in 2008 claimed over 1,000 lives. Later, the Waki Commission revealed that reconnaissance for violence had been underway well in advance, criminals were organising, and funding was increasing; despite receiving early warnings, state intelligence failed to take effective action. Eastern Ukraine experienced a comparable pattern: in 2014, initial reconnaissance operations to seize government buildings in Donetsk and Luhansk were relatively small. Large-scale armed operations began only after assessing how quickly Kyiv responded and which way local police leaned.

“Sheikh Hasina will return”—alright. Yet what connection does this have with 49 crude bomb explosions and seven vehicle arson attacks in the capital during the first eight days of November alone? What is the link with the “burn down factories” campaign infiltrating ready-made garment workers’ protests? What explains the nationwide arson attacks on Grameen Bank branches and the burning down of an NCP female leader’s home? What drives the spread of violence nationwide—padlocking courts and educational institutions, petrol bombs, explosions, arson, and vandalism?

Law enforcement agencies have set up 252 checkpoints across the capital and nationwide. Police state that some individuals are leaving their own localities to commit sabotage elsewhere, and several have been identified and arrested.

Multiple indicators suggest these are “test cases”:

First, the nationwide spread of violence. Within a span of just one or two days, incidents erupted from Cox’s Bazar to Rajshahi, and from Khagrachhari to Barguna. Isolated grievances do not spread simultaneously and uniformly across so many districts.

Second, the diversity of targets. Not merely buses and trucks, but trains, the Padma Bridge entrance, areas outside airports, UNO offices, courts, universities, and the symbolically significant Dhanmondi 32. Each target corresponds to a distinct security capability marker of the state—probing highway police, railway security, Key Point Installation (KPI) protection, airport security, and administrative security infrastructure.

Third, symbolic messaging. Targeting Grameen Bank branches is no coincidence; it probes how strongly the government reacts when symbols associated with Muhammad Yunus are attacked.

Fourth, hired operatives. Those caught setting off explosives do not know one another, nor do they know who hired them. This is a textbook example of probing, allowing perpetrators to keep their core network intact.

Fifth, border reconnaissance. The government itself could not determine how former MP Ranjit Sarkar entered Sunamganj to hold a meeting. The Inspector General of Police (IGP) has instructed Superintendents of Police (SPs) across all districts to step up patrols and intelligence surveillance in border areas to prevent infiltration. The Home Minister himself alleged in Parliament that vast sums of money and incitement are flowing in from across the border.

Is there an active attempt to spark a civil war?

This hypothesis is not meant to spread panic, but to alert the state apparatus after observing clear signs of probing. The violence remains at an embryonic stage, yet within this probing, one senses a concerted effort to provoke the opposing side and drag the country toward confrontation. 

The nation is visibly polarised into two camps: staunch supporters of Sheikh Hasina on one side, and staunch anti-Hasina forces on the other. In other words, the gunpowder for a fratricidal civil war is already laid; it merely awaits a lit matchstick.

I see a real risk—and what is the reasoning? The reasoning lies in the lessons of history:

First, Loss of Power and Status: In her book How Civil Wars Start, Barbara Walter demonstrates that civil wars are most frequently initiated by groups that once sat at the centre of power and suddenly lost their authority, status, and strength. Being banned, excluded from elections, and facing a death sentence for their top leader are all hallmarks of such loss.

2. Anocracy (Intermediate Transition): Barbara Walter’s research also indicates that countries transitioning from one political system to another—rather than full democracies or full autocracies—face the highest risk. Following the 2024 Mass Uprising, the interim government, the February 2026 election, and a major party losing its right to contest elections, Bangladesh serves as a textbook example of an anocratic transitional phase.

3. Counter-Violence and Vigilante Patrols: Retaliatory attacks have occurred on the homes of Awami League activists in Netrokona, while activists of the BNP and allied parties have patrolled streets with bamboo poles in Mirpur, Mohammadpur, Farmgate, and Tejgaon in Dhaka. When party cadres assume security duties in place of the state, a vicious cycle of action and retaliation ensues.

4. Symbolic Timing: December is the month of Victory, and it also marks the anniversary of attacks on Prothom Alo, The Daily Star, Chhayanaut, and Udichi following the death of Sharif Osman Hadi. Moreover, it is the first Victory Day during the tenure of the incumbent BNP government. The symbolic weight of choosing this timeframe is undeniable.

5. Strategic Exploitation of Economic Grievances: The Home Minister has surely spoken knowingly in stating that funds from “fallen forces” are infiltrating even the legitimate protests of garment workers. When grievances have an economic foundation, political incitement easily gains traction.

6. Easy Availability of Firearms: A portion of the weapons looted from police stations in August 2024 remains unrecovered. Ignoring this threat would be foolish.

7. Overt Provocation: India’s BJP MP Nishikant Dubey has spoken of “taking back” Noakhali, Sylhet, and Chattogram Port. While he is not a spokesperson for the Indian government, such remarks serve as direct provocation to inflame ultra-nationalist tensions inside Bangladesh.

Is Sheikh Hasina’s return actually possible?

For Sheikh Hasina to return normally through an airport as a free citizen with a passport is entirely impossible. Realistically, only two avenues remain open to her: returning as a prisoner via extradition, or returning voluntarily to surrender and face arrest. The reasons are crystal clear.

On 17 November 2025, the International Crimes Tribunal-1 sentenced her to death in absentia, with the full verdict published on 13 January. Under Section 21 of the Tribunal Act, the timeframe for filing an appeal is 30 days, and Section 21(3) bars the acceptance of belated appeals. No appeal was lodged on her behalf within the stipulated period.

This means she has exhausted all legal remedies; upon returning or being arrested, the sentence will take effect. If she returns, she must surrender, yet returning does not guarantee the right to appeal. She might have glimpsed a faint ray of hope for a minor exception, but recent violence orchestrated by her party has extinguished even that last glimmer. Abul Kalam Azad, convicted by the same tribunal, filed a petition seeking condonation of delay for a late appeal, which remains pending before the Appellate Division. A favourable ruling from the Appellate Division could have set a precedent applicable to Sheikh Hasina. But the court may no longer be inclined toward leniency.

Sheikh Hasina has fallen into the trap of laws crafted by her own administration. The original 1973 Act contained no provision for trials in absentia; in 2012, the Awami League amended the law specifically to cripple opposition politics. Without that amendment, the court could not have tried or sentenced her to death in absentia—or if it had, the verdict would have rested on weak legal footing.

Similarly, in the 2013 amendment, Sheikh Hasina’s government introduced the state’s right to appeal against verdicts to eliminate political adversaries—an amendment used to convert Abdul Quader Molla’s life sentence into the death penalty. Even if Sheikh Hasina’s death sentence were somehow commuted to life imprisonment through a legal loophole, it would yield little benefit, as the state could exercise that very right of appeal to reinstate the death penalty.

Nor do international bodies or human rights organisations hold any jurisdiction to commute Hasina’s sentence to life imprisonment. Numerous anti-death penalty organisations and the UN Human Rights Council itself urged her government in 2013 to abolish capital punishment or commute tribunal death sentences to life terms—requests Sheikh Hasina’s government flatly rejected. Had even a single precedent been set back then, she could have benefited from it today.

Furthermore, Sheikh Hasina has forfeited the legal right to obtain a passport, travel pass, or National Identity Card. A state is under no obligation to issue travel documents to a convicted fugitive. Without a passport or travel pass, she has no legal avenue to travel to a third country unless that nation issues her exceptional documentation on its own initiative—something no country will do given that a UN investigation has corroborated her culpability in the killing of citizens.

Could India grant her citizenship? That, too, is impossible. Under Section 6 and the Third Schedule of India’s Citizenship Act, 1955, naturalisation requires continuous residence in India for the 12 months preceding application, plus at least 11 years out of the previous 14 years. Hasina has been in India for just over two years. Meanwhile, the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) of 2019 reduced the residency requirement to five years exclusively for Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan—completely excluding Muslims. As a Muslim, the CAA route is entirely closed to her.

India’s assertion that she has been sheltered on “humanitarian” grounds has also complicated her extradition. Even if New Delhi wished to hand her over to reset relations with Bangladesh or honour the extradition treaty, it would struggle to do so. International human rights bodies would fiercely condemn India, arguing that sending a “humanitarian” asylum seeker to face an “inhumane” death penalty is not only unethical, but unjust and unlawful.

Although Article 6 of the extradition treaty permits refusing extradition for offences of a “political character,” India cannot invoke that clause either, because the same treaty explicitly excludes murder, attempted murder, and incitement to murder from the definition of political offences. Thus, India cannot publicly claim she was granted refuge as a victim of “political vendetta.” This Catch-22 situation puts India in a bind as well: legally, the treaty obliges India to extradite Sheikh Hasina, yet doing so remains practically impossible.

Do Awami League activists truly believe Sheikh Hasina will return?

Most party activists and supporters firmly believe that Sheikh Hasina will inevitably return, though none possess a clear idea of how. Back in July, Prothom Alo noted uncertainty even within party ranks over whether this was a genuine plan or merely a tactic to keep grassroots morale alive. Despite calls after the parliamentary election in February for exiled leaders to return home, not a single senior leader responded.

In his book When Prophecy Fails, social psychologist Leon Festinger observed a religious cult and demonstrated that when a prediction fails to materialise on the appointed date, followers do not abandon their faith—instead, they proselytise even more fervently to resolve their “cognitive dissonance”. Once December passes without Hasina’s return, a segment of her most dedicated followers will grow disillusioned and drift away. However, another faction will construct a new narrative: “She was prevented from returning by a conspiracy.”It is this second faction that risks becoming the vanguard of violence.

Suppose she actually returns, faces arrest, and meets execution. What follows? The first possibility is the fate of the Muslim League (political irrelevance). The second possibility is armed civil war—her demise viewed as martyrdom by devoted cadres, sparking armed retaliatory groups fuelled by unchecked emotion. Some quarters may actively desire this very “pretext,” as a death sentence generates an emotional surge that no organisational programme could ever match. The third possibility is even more perilous: escalating orchestrated chaos, leading to greater bloodshed and, ultimately, the spectre of military rule.

How prepared is the govt to confront the danger?

The Home Minister remarked that a single crude bomb exploding on a car roof outside a university at midnight does not signify a breakdown of law and order. A few weeks earlier, following a flash procession, he stated there was no scope to label the police’s role a failure.

I am not suggesting the government lacks preparation or is underprepared. The IGP has convened meetings with SPs across all 64 districts and Range DIGs, issuing directives to intensify patrols, border surveillance, and intelligence operations. Additional police have been deployed in Gopalganj, Shariatpur, Madaripur, and Faridpur, alongside six platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) in Gopalganj. Nationwide, 252 checkpoints have been set up, while Industrial Police and BGB are operating jointly in industrial zones. What truly needs examining is the nature of the state’s preparedness.

Thus far, the government’s response has been predominantly reactive—arrests and checkpoints after incidents occur. There is little visible evidence of a proactive, intelligence-led strategy focused on tracing and severing financial pipelines.

In security policy, “saving face” is the most expensive luxury. Experiences in Kenya and Rwanda demonstrate that a major reason warning signs were ignored was political leaders’ fear that visible, large-scale mobilisation might make the government appear weak or fearful, inviting public ridicule.

A reliable government remains steadfast in the principle that “prevention is better than cure.” The administration must undertake comprehensive security preparations, yet without adopting a belligerent posture. 

Crude rhetoric insinuating that “the government has the legal authority for crossfire or police killings if it wishes” must cease immediately. As an analysis in Asia Times aptly warned, if authorities respond with indiscriminate arrests or excessive force, a security challenge can swiftly morph into another full-blown political conflict. The Home Minister himself has stated that conspiracies will be foiled strictly within the bounds of human rights.

Human rights boundaries must certainly not be crossed by even a fraction. However, in crafting a “preparedness policy,” the word “conspiracy” ought to be discarded. The casual, meaningless overuse of this word has become something of an ailment among Bangladeshi politicians.

For effective preparedness, politics must be viewed as a chessboard. When one player makes a move and the opponent plans a counter-move, do we say the opponent is “conspiring”? Likewise in politics, rivals are not “conspiring”—they are calculating which counter-move will checkmate their adversary.

An indispensable goal of this preparedness policy must be elevating Bangladesh’s intelligence capabilities to international standards. Recent acts of violence have starkly exposed intelligence failures.

Lastly

Sheikh Hasina’s return as a free citizen is virtually impossible. While the suspicion that a third party is seeking to instigate a civil war may sound somewhat hyperbolic, it cannot be ruled out entirely. For now, the violence remains low-intensity and within manageable limits—yet “protracted low-intensity political violence” can easily spiral into a “vicious cycle of revenge.” The risk is real.

Whether the current wave of sabotage forms part of a third party’s capability-testing project remains unproven, even though government spokespersons themselves are pointing fingers at a third party. Consequently, the state’s preparedness must match the adversary move for move. The danger lies not in any isolated incident, but in a chain reaction of events—each provoking the next.

Historically, almost every civil war began following a trigger event, escalating through overreaction, counter-reaction, and bloody struggles by military or civilian political factions exploiting chaos to seize state authority. If a third party desires a civil war, their sharpest weapons will be state miscalculation, complacency, overconfidence, and utter indifference.

* Helal Mohiuddin is a faculty member in Liberal Arts at Mayville State University, North Dakota, USA

* Views expressed are the author’s own
